lead: Every XML layout is a tree of views, and most view attributes map to a setter: android:text → setText, android:visibility → setVisibility. Attributes that start with layout_ do not; they belong to the parent's LayoutParams, so you set them with new LinearLayout.LayoutParams(...) or by calling setLayoutParams. Java can build the same tree with new TextView(this), setText and addView, which helps when rows are dynamic, such as one row per UPI transaction. A touch becomes a callback through one fixed path: dispatchTouchEvent → onTouchEvent → performClick → your onClick. Only a few universities teach programmatic UI; it is worth knowing because it makes sizes, weights and listeners explicit.
prereq: You need 3.1 for LayoutParams and weights, and 3.4 for listeners on buttons and lists.

blocks.text: Create the root, create each child, set its properties, attach LayoutParams, add the child, then pass the root to setContentView. Sizes are pixels unless you convert. The display density is getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density; at density 3, 1 dp is 3 px.

items: TextView t = new TextView(this); t.setText("Balance"); t.setTextSize(16); t.setPadding(16, 8, 16, 8);

blocks.where: px is the pixel value passed to setPadding; dp is the design size; density is getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density, for example 3 on a high-density phone.

blocks.text: setTextSize(16) uses sp by default. setPadding takes px. A view made in code has no LayoutParams until you set them. With addView(view) and no params, the parent uses its default LayoutParams: wrap_content × wrap_content when the LinearLayout is horizontal, match_parent × wrap_content when it is vertical. Weight can only be set through explicit LinearLayout.LayoutParams, so it silently does nothing here.

A click can be wired in three ways. In XML, android:onClick="onButtonClick" needs a public void onButtonClick(View v) method in the activity. In Java, use an anonymous class: b.setOnClickListener(new View.OnClickListener(){ public void onClick(View v){ ... } });. Or let the activity implement View.OnClickListener and call b.setOnClickListener(this).

items: A tap reaches dispatchTouchEvent first, which sends the event down the view tree.
The view's onTouchEvent returns true to consume the touch, then performClick runs, then your onClick.
If onTouchEvent returns false, the view does not consume the touch, so the parent may handle it and your click may not fire.
Text fields notify through a TextWatcher; afterTextChanged(Editable s) runs after each change.
Log.d("TAG", "clicked") confirms that a listener fired; v.getId() tells you which view.

figure.caption: Three buttons built in code, each with width 0 and weight 1, share a 360 dp row, so each takes 120 dp of space (360 px at density 3). Tapping the second button hands the listener a View whose id is 101, so the index is 101 − 100 = 1.

spec.title: Three weight-1 buttons on a 360 dp row
spec.aria: A row of three buttons on a 360 dp screen: ids 100, 101 and 102, each 120 dp wide which is 360 px at density 3, with the middle button tapped so the listener receives id 101 at index 1.

examples.question: A horizontal LinearLayout on a 360 dp screen will hold three buttons. Each button has layout width 0 and weight 1. Button i gets id 100 + i, and all three share one OnClickListener. The user taps the second button. What is each button's width, and what does the listener receive? Use density 3.
steps: This snippet only computes the widths and the tapped id; the LinearLayout, Button, LayoutParams and listener calls are shown in Section 1.
Root width = 360 dp. There are 3 equal weights, so each weight unit gets 360 ÷ 3 = 120 dp.
Each button width = 120 dp because width 0 plus weight 1 gives all space by weight.
Convert to pixels: px = dp × density = 120 × 3 = 360 px per button.
Tapped button is the second, so i = 1 and its id = 100 + 1 = 101.
The listener receives v, the tapped View. v.getId() returns 101.
examples.answer: Each button is 120 dp (360 px) wide, and the listener receives the second button's View, whose id is 101 and index is 1.
examples.check:
screen_dp=360
n=3
density=3
each_dp=screen_dp//n
each_px=each_dp*density
tapped_id=100+1
index=tapped_id-100
print(each_dp)
print(each_px)
print(tapped_id)
print(index)

traps: A view created in code has no LayoutParams until you set them; addView(view) with no params uses the parent's default LayoutParams (wrap_content × wrap_content in a horizontal LinearLayout, match_parent × wrap_content in a vertical one), and weights silently do nothing.
The XML onClick method must be public, return void and take exactly one View argument, or the app crashes on the first tap.
setPadding takes pixels, not dp; convert with density first or spacing looks too small.
onTouchEvent returning false means the view does not consume the touch, so performClick and your onClick may not run.
setTextSize(16) means 16 sp, not 16 dp; do not treat text size and padding units as the same.

quiz.q: What three properties must an android:onClick method have?
quiz.a: It must be public, return void, and take exactly one View parameter.

quiz.q: Why does addView(view) without LayoutParams break weights?
quiz.a: Without params the parent uses its default LayoutParams, which has no weight value set (for LinearLayout: wrap_content × wrap_content when horizontal, match_parent × wrap_content when vertical). Weight only applies through an explicit LinearLayout.LayoutParams with width 0 and the weight.

quiz.q: Density is 2.5. Convert 24 dp to px for setPadding.
Three buttons have width 0 and weight 1 on a 480 dp row. What is each width in dp?
A custom view returns false from onTouchEvent. What happens to the click listener?
quiz.a: The view does not consume the touch, so performClick may not run and the parent may handle the event; the click listener may not fire.

quiz.q: Which callback reports typing in an EditText?
quiz.a: TextWatcher.afterTextChanged(Editable s) runs after each change.

quiz.q: Which log call writes a debug message with a tag?

beyond: Not for the exam. Programmatic UI is the base for Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI, where you describe state and the framework rebuilds views. Industry teams test listeners with UI tests and accessibility checks, not only Log.d. Search for Android input event dispatch, ViewConfiguration touch slop, and Compose state hoisting next.
